# Language verbosity

<!-- @generated by tools/verbosity. Do not edit by hand. -->

How much source text each profiled language needs for the same work, measured on
[mal](https://github.com/kanaka/mal) at revision `2bbfaa54cca4908efc90b4173b1406e260788e8a`.

The corpus is licensed under the Mozilla Public License 2.0. Entl redistributes no corpus source
either way: the tool reads a checkout the operator downloads, and only the
statistics on this page and in `crates/entl-codebase/src/profiles/verbosity.rs`
are checked in.

## Method

1. A solution is reduced to program text: comments are removed using the
   language's own `CommentSyntax` from its Entl profile, blank lines are
   dropped, and each remaining line is trimmed so indentation style does not
   read as verbosity. String literals are kept — they are program content.
2. Each language contributes exactly one unit: its **whole implementation**, every source file under `impls/<lang>` except tests and build scripts. Finer units were tried and rejected — implementations factor differently, and matching files by name credits nobody for the hash map Zig had to write itself. Whole implementations count every byte exactly once.
3. Every language implements the one unit, so each pair is compared directly
   and there is nothing to average over.

Corpus: one implementation per language, 16 of Entl's language profiles. Languages with no algorithmic presence in the corpus — HTML, CSS,
JSON, YAML, TOML, Markdown, Dockerfile, Vue, Svelte — carry no measurement at
all.

## Index

Every language is measured on the one shared unit and normalized so
`c` is 1.0, so the index is that measurement rather than a fit over
many. No deviation column is shown: with a single unit the ratios are exactly
transitive and every residual is zero by arithmetic, and there is no spread
here to put an error bar on.

## How far from transitive

Not at all, and that is arithmetic rather than a result. Every pair is derived
from the same sixteen measurements, so composing two ratios reproduces the third
exactly and the least-squares fit has nothing to reconcile. The transitivity
check and the balanced panel that the collection corpora report are omitted
here: with one shared unit they would be measuring the identity.

What this corpus cannot tell you is how much of its disagreement with the
others is size and how much is genre. One program is one genre, and this one is
an interpreter — tagged unions, recursion, and manual memory management for a
garbage-collected target. Separating the two would take several mid-sized
programs implemented in the same set of languages.

## What this does not measure

The corpus is small, self-contained tasks. That rewards a terse standard library
and charges any language that requires declarations, imports, or a class to hold
`main` — real costs, but ones that amortize away in a large program and so
overstate the gap at scale.

Solutions are contributed, not controlled, and they do not all answer the same
question. Ackermann in C ships the function plus a `main` that prints a table;
Ackermann in Ruby ships the function. Both are valid entries; only one includes
a driver. Taking the median across a task's solutions damps this, but it does
not remove it, and it runs the same direction as the ceremony it is measured
alongside: the languages that need a `main` are the ones whose contributors
tend to write one.

Two more, smaller: the corpus files Kotlin solutions as scripts, which skip
ceremony a Kotlin application file carries; and languages near the task floor
(`typescript`, `zig`, `sql`) rest on few enough shared tasks that a handful of
entries moves them, which is what their deviation figures are reporting.

None of this is a statement about readability, maintainability, or how long a
task takes to write.
